			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We use </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Adjusted EBITDA to evaluate our operating performance and as a measure of performance for incentive compensation purposes. Additionally, our credit facilities use Adjusted EBITDA, subject to further permitted adjustments, for certain financial covenants. We believe Adjusted EBITDA </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">is a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> measure of performance used by some investors, equity analysts, rating agencies and lenders to make informed decisions as to, among other things, our ability to incur and service debt and make capital expenditures. In addition, multiples of current or projected Adjusted EBITDA are used by some investors and equity analysts to estimate current or prospective enterprise value. Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> measure</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> of financial performance under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (&#x201C;GAAP&#x201D;), and the items excluded from Adjusted EBITDA are significant components in understanding and assessing financial performance. Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered in isolation or as an alternative to net income, cash flows generated by operating, investing or financing activities or other financial statement data presented in the consolidated financial statements as an indicator of financial performance. Because Adjusted EBITDA </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">is </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">not </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a measurement</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> determined in accordance with GAAP and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">is </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">susceptible to varying calculations, Adjusted EBITDA as presented may not be comparable to other similarly titled measures of other companies.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Refer to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;Certain Definitions&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> above for a description of how we define Adjusted EBITDA.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">For the Years Ended </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">December 31, 2017 and 2016</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">During the </font><font style="display: inline;">year </font><font style="display: inline;">ended December 31, 2017, we recorded an increase to our provision for doubtful accounts of $72.6 million, $46.0 million net of income taxes, or $1.1</font><font style="display: inline;">3</font><font style="display: inline;"> loss per diluted share, as a result of a change in our accounting estimate of the collectability of accounts receivable.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">We are in the process of installing new systems, developing enhanced analytical procedures and updating our estimation processes in order to centralize and standardize our processes for estimating the collectability of these accounts.&nbsp; In connection with these implementation efforts, we identified additional information which indicated that our current collection estimates might be different from our historical collection estimates. We utilized this new information to further refine our estimation procedures to more precisely estimate the collectability of accounts receivable at a more detailed and disaggregated level.&nbsp; The change in our estimation procedures of the collectability of our accounts receivable is considered a change in accounting estimate in accordance with ASC 250-10.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Throughout the discussion of our operating results for the year ended December 31, 2017, we have provided certain metrics as a percentage of revenues and other revenue-related ratios on an adjusted basis excluding the impact of the $72.6 million change in accounting estimate in order to yield greater comparability in our operating results for the year ended December 31, 2017 compared to the prior year.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

When adjusted to exclude the impact of the transfer of home health and hospice service lines to IHHP, which we do not consolidate, our same-hospital revenues before provision for doubtful accounts increased $76.1 million, or 1.1% </font><font style="display: inline;">for the </font><font style="display: inline;">year </font><font style="display: inline;">ended December 31, 2017 compared to the </font><font style="display: inline;">prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">primarily a result of higher contracted rates from HMOs, PPOs and other private insurers, partially offset by a shift from HMOs, PPOs and other private insurers to Medicare and Medicaid for a portion of our patient population. </font><font style="display: inline;">Additionally, </font><font style="display: inline;">our same-h</font><font style="display: inline;">ospital equivalent admissions decreased by</font><font style="display: inline;"> 0.9% </font><font style="display: inline;">for the </font><font style="display: inline;">year</font><font style="display: inline;"> ended December 31, 2017 compared to the </font><font style="display: inline;">prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year. </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Our </font><font style="display: inline;">same-hospital </font><font style="display: inline;">equivalent admissions were negatively impacted by decreases in admissions, surgical volumes and emergency room visits during the </font><font style="display: inline;">year</font><font style="display: inline;"> ended December 31, 2017 compared to the </font><font style="display: inline;">prior year. </font>

		<p style="margin:10pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">For the year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;">, our salaries and benefits expense </font><font style="display: inline;">increased</font><font style="display: inline;"> to $</font><font style="display: inline;">3,056.4</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, or </font><font style="display: inline;">0.3</font><font style="display: inline;">%, compared to $</font><font style="display: inline;">3,047.4</font><font style="display: inline;"> million for the prior year</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;This increase was primarily driven by the use of more expensive contract nursing labor in certain of our markets and the increasing cost of employing a greater number of physicians and their related support staff as evidenced by a 1.6% increase in our salaries and benefits per equivalent admission for the year ended December 31, 2017 compared to the prior year.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, this increase was partially driven by one additional month of operations for Providence during the year ended December 31, 2017 compared to the prior year.&nbsp;&nbsp;These increases were partially offset by the sale of Rockdale and labor costs associated with</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">home health and hospice service lines being transferred to IHHP, which we do not consolidate. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:10pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">When adjusted to exclude the impact of the $72.6 million </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">increase </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">recorded </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">to the provision for doubtful accounts</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">during the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">year ended December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> as a result of a change in accounting estimate</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, our salaries and benefits expense for the year ended December 31, 2017 represented 48.0% of revenues, compared to 47.9% of revenues for the prior year.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">For </font><font style="display: inline;">the year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> our other operating expenses </font><font style="display: inline;">decreased</font><font style="display: inline;"> to $</font><font style="display: inline;">1,521.3</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, or </font><font style="display: inline;">2.4</font><font style="display: inline;">%, compared to $</font><font style="display: inline;">1,558.1</font><font style="display: inline;"> million for the prior year</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">primarily as a result of</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">decreases in our insurance expenses and other operating </font><font style="display: inline;">expenses, partially offset by</font><font style="display: inline;"> increase</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> in </font><font style="display: inline;">non-income taxes and </font><font style="display: inline;">professional fees.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our insurance expenses were higher for the year ended December 31, 2016</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> primarily as a result of recording an accrual for loss contingencies of $24.7 million for cardiology-related legal proceedings</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> as described further in Note 12 to our accompanying consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this report</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> and lower for the year ended December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> as a result of favorable claims development under our self-insured professional liability program</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, our other operating expenses decreased during the year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31</font><font style="display: inline;">, 2017 </font><font style="display: inline;">primarily as a result of lower legal and consulting fees and the positive financial performance of certain non-consolidated businesses.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Our non-income taxes were </font><font style="display: inline;">lower during the </font><font style="display: inline;">year </font><font style="display: inline;">ended December 31, 2016 </font><font style="display: inline;">due </font><font style="display: inline;">to favorable </font><font style="display: inline;">gross receipts</font><font style="display: inline;"> tax adjustments in certain of our markets</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Lastly, as a result of a continued shortage of physicians in many of our communities, we have experienced increasing professional fees in areas such as anesthesiology and hospitalists, in addition to higher subsidies under certain of our professional arrangements where we guarantee minimum levels of service.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:10pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">When adjusted to exclude the impact of the $72.6 million </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">increase </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">recorded </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">to the provision for doubtful accounts during the</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> year ended December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> as a result of a change in accounting estimate</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, our other operating expenses for the year ended December 31, 2017 represented 23.9% of revenues, compared to 24.5% of revenues for the same period last year.</font>

The debt transaction costs include the write-offs of previously capitalized issuance costs and new non-capital costs related to our various debt transactions entered into during the year ended December 31, 2016.</font>

		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Provision for Income Taxes</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our provision for income taxes was $46.9 million, or 0.7% of revenues, for the year ended December 31, 2017, compared to $73.0 million, or 1.1% of revenues, for the prior year.&nbsp; The de</font><font style="display: inline;">crease in the provision for income taxes for </font><font style="display: inline;">the year ended December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;"> was primarily attributable to </font><font style="display: inline;">a decrease in our income before income taxes </font><font style="display: inline;">for the year ended December 31, 2017 compared to the prior year,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">in addition to a decrease in our effective tax rate</font><font style="display: inline;"> to 31.4% for the year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;"> compared to 37.5% for the prior year</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">When</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> adjusted to </font><font style="display: inline;">exclude the </font><font style="display: inline;">increase </font><font style="display: inline;">to the provision for doubtful accounts as a result of a change in accounting estimate, </font><font style="display: inline;">other non-operating gains and losses </font><font style="display: inline;">and the impact of the Tax Act</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, our </font><font style="display: inline;">effective tax rate</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> for the year ended December 31, 2017 was </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">comparable to </font><font style="display: inline;">the prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Additionally, on December 22, 2017, the Tax Act was signed into law. The Tax Act significantly revises the U.S. corporate income tax by, among other things, lowering the statutory corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% and eliminating certain deductions</font><font style="display: inline;">. Due to the timing of the enactment and the complexity involved in applying the provisions of the Tax Act</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">we have </font><font style="display: inline;">made reasonable estimates of the effects of the Tax Act on our existing deferred tax assets and liabilities and recognized a provisional benefit for income taxes of $18.0 million, or $0.44 earnings per diluted share, for the year ended December 31, 2017. As we complete our analysis of the Tax Act, including the collection of data and interpretation of any additional guidance issued by the U.S. Treasury Department, the IRS, and other standard-setting bodies, we may make adjustments to the provisional amounts. Those adjustments may materially impact our provision for income taxes in the period in which the adjustments are made.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our provision for doubtful accounts relates principally to amounts due from patients included in our self-pay population and other amounts such as co-payments and deductibles due from</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> patients included in other paye</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">r categories. For the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">year </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ended </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Dec</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ember 3</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">1</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, 2016, our provision for doubtful accounts increased by $</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">109.5</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> million, or </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">13.7</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">%, to $</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">909.6</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> million on a consolidated basis compared to the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">prior</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> year. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">This increase was primarily a result of our 2016 and 2015 acquisitions.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">The provision and allowance for doubtful accounts are critical accounting estimates and are further discussed in Part II, Item 7. </font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations</font><font style="display: inline;">, &#x201C;Critical Accounting Estimates.&#x201D;</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">For the year ended December 31, 2016, our other operating expenses increased to $1,558.1 million, or 25.0%, compared to $1,246.4 million for the prior year primarily as a result of our 2016 and </font><font style="display: inline;">2015 acquisitions as well as increases in our professional fees, contract services and insurance expenses. As a result of a continued shortage of physicians in many of our communities, we have experienced increasing professional fees in areas such as anesthesiology and hospitalists. Additionally, our contract services expenses have increased primarily as a result of higher business office collection efforts arising from an increase in revenues as well as additional contract services associated with an increasing number of employed physicians. Lastly, we experienced an increase in our insurance expenses for the year ended December 31, 2016 as a result of recording an accrual for loss contingencies of $24.7 million for cardiology-related legal proceedings as described further in Note 12 to our accompanying consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this report.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Liquidity</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our primary sources of liquidity are cash flows provided by our operations and our debt borrowings.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Senior Credit Agreement matures on June 10, 2021 and provides for a $700.0 million senior secured term loan facility (the &#x201C;Term Facility&#x201D;) and a $600.0 million senior secured revolving credit facility (the &#x201C;Revolving Facility&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;Throughout 2017, we borrowed and subsequently repaid </font><font style="display: inline;">$205.0 million</font><font style="display: inline;"> under the Revolving Facility for general corporate purposes.&nbsp;&nbsp;We believe that our internally generated cash flows and amounts available for borrowing under our Senior Credit Agreement will be adequate to service existing debt, finance internal growth and fund capital expenditures and small to mid-size hospital acquisitions over the next twelve months and into the foreseeable future prior to maturity dates of our outstanding debt. Certain larger hospital acquisitions may, however, require additional financing.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The non-GAAP metric of free operating cash flow is an important liquidity measure for us. Our computation of free operating cash flow consists of net cash provided by operating activities less cash flows used for the purchase of property and equipment.&nbsp;&nbsp;We believe that free operating cash flow is useful to investors and management as a measure of the ability of our business to generate cash and to repay and incur additional debt. Free operating cash flow does not fully reflect our ability to freely deploy generated cash, as it does not reflect required debt payments or other fixed obligations. Computations of free operating cash flow may differ from company to company. Therefore, free operating cash flow should be used as a complement to, and in conjunction with, our consolidated statements of cash flows presented in our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this report.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Refer to the table above for a reconciliation of free operating cash flow to net cash provided by operating activities, the most comparable GAAP measure.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our cash flows provided by operating activities for the </font><font style="display: inline;">year </font><font style="display: inline;">ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017 </font><font style="display: inline;">compared to 2016 </font><font style="display: inline;">were positively impacted by increases in the amount and </font><font style="display: inline;">differences in </font><font style="display: inline;">the timing of cash collections of outstanding accounts receivable, partially offset by increases in the amount and </font><font style="display: inline;">differences in </font><font style="display: inline;">the timing of cash payments for self-insurance claims, income taxes, accounts payable and accrued expenses.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:13.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our cash flows provided by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2016 compared to 2015 were negatively impacted by the timing of cash collections of outstanding accounts receivable primarily as a result of the normal revenue cycle build-up of accounts receivable at certain of our recently acquired hospitals where we did not acquire outstanding accounts receivable.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, our cash flows provided by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2016 as compared to 2015 were negatively impacted by increases in the amount and </font><font style="display: inline;">differences in </font><font style="display: inline;">the </font><font style="display: inline;">timing of payments for income taxes and interest and a decrease in the amount and </font><font style="display: inline;">differences in </font><font style="display: inline;">the </font><font style="display: inline;">timing of receipts related to certain Medicaid DSH programs</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;"> These decreases were partially offset by decreases in the amount and </font><font style="display: inline;">differences in </font><font style="display: inline;">the </font><font style="display: inline;">timing of payments for accounts payable and accrued salaries.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">We have a formal and intensive review procedure for the authorization of capital expenditures that exceed an established threshold. One of the most important financial measures of acceptability for a discretionary capital project is whether its projected discounted cash flow return on investment exceeds our projected cost of capital for that project. We expect to continue to invest in information systems, modern technologies, emergency room and operating room expansions, the construction of medical office buildings for physician expansion and the reconfiguration of the flow of patient care.&nbsp; Additionally, we may from time to time replace existing hospital buildings with new buildings as we evaluate ongoing repair and maintenance costs and other factors that impact the future operations of the existing buildings. </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Liquidity and Capital Resources Outlook</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We expect total capital expenditures to </font><font style="display: inline;">continue to be elevated and in a range of</font><font style="display: inline;"> $475.0 million and $500.0 million for 2018</font><font style="display: inline;">, primarily</font><font style="display: inline;"> a result of ongoing capital commitments in connection with several of our acquired facilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;As part of </font><font style="display: inline;">our </font><font style="display: inline;">current acquisition strategy, </font><font style="display: inline;">we</font><font style="display: inline;"> expect capital expenditure commitments to be a significant component of future acquisitions.</font><font style="display: inline;"> &nbsp;At December 31, 2017, we estimated our total remaining capital expenditure commitments, including commitments for routine projects, to be approximately $1,305.1 million, which generally have remaining terms of </font><font style="display: inline;">four to eight years.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">At </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017</font><font style="display: inline;">, we had uncompleted projects with an estimated addit</font><font style="display: inline;">ional cost to complete</font><font style="display: inline;"> of approximately $</font><font style="display: inline;">358.7</font><font style="display: inline;"> million.</font><font style="display: inline;"> The estimated timeframe for completion of these projects generally ranges from less than one year up to three years. We anticipate funding these expenditures through cash provided by operating activities, available cash and borrowings available under the Senior Credit Agreement.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:14.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our business strategy contemplates the selective acquisition of additional hospitals and other healthcare service providers, and we regularly review potential acquisitions. These acquisitions may, however, require additional financing. We regularly evaluate opportunities to sell additional equity or debt securities, obtain credit agreements from lenders or restructure our long-term debt or equity for strategic reasons or to further strengthen our financial position. The sale of additional equity or convertible debt securities could result in additional dilution to our stockholders.</font>
		</p>

Certain larger hospital acquisitions may, however, require additional financing.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The following discussion of critical accounting estimates is not intended to be a comprehensive list of all of our accounting p</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">olicies that require estimates, but </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the estimates discussed below involve a higher degree of judgment and complexity. We believe the current assumptions and other considerations used to estimate amounts reflected in our consolidated financial statements are appropriate. However, if actual experience differs from the assumptions and other considerations used in estimating amounts reflected in our consolidated financial statements, the resulting changes could have a material adverse effect on our consolidated results of operations and our financial condition.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The discussion that follows presents information about our critical accounting estimates, as well as the effects of hypothetical changes in the material assumptions used to develop each estimate.</font>

		<p style="margin:5pt 20.9pt 12pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Revenue Recognition and Accounts Receivable</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We recognize revenues in the period in which services are provided. Accounts receivable primarily consist of a</font><font style="display: inline;">mounts due from third-party paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs and patients. Our ability to collect outstanding receivables is critical to our results of operations and cash flows. Amounts we receive for treatment of patients covered by governmental programs, such as Medicare and Medi</font><font style="display: inline;">caid, and other third-party paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs such as HMOs, PPOs and other private insurers, are generally less than our established billing rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, to provide for accounts receivable that could become uncollectible in the future, we establish an allowance for doubtful accounts to reduce the carrying value of such receivables to their estimated net realizable value.&nbsp;&nbsp;Accordingly, our revenues and accounts receivable are reduced to net realizable value through an allowance for contractual discounts and a provision for doubtful accounts.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Revenues are recorded at estimated net amounts due</font><font style="display: inline;"> from patients, third-party paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs and others for healthcare ser</font><font style="display: inline;">vices provided. For certain paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs, such as Medicare, Medicaid, a</font><font style="display: inline;">s well as some managed care paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs with which we have contractual arrangements, the contractual allowances are calculated by computerized logging systems based on defin</font><font style="display: inline;">ed payment terms. For other paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs, the contractual allowances are determined based on historical data by insurance plan. All contractual adjustm</font><font style="display: inline;">ents, regardless of type of paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r or method of calculation, are reviewed and compared to actual experience.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Medicare and Medicaid</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The majority of services performed on Medicare and Medicaid patients are reimbursed at predetermined reimbursement rates. The differences between the established billing rates (i.e., gross charges) and the predetermined reimbursement rates are recorded as contractual discounts and deducted from gross charges. Under the Medicaid program&#x2019;s prospective reimbursement systems, there is no adjustment or settlement of the difference between the actual cost to provide the service and the predetermined reimbursement rates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Discounts for retrospectively cost-based revenues are estimated based on historical and current factors and are adjusted in future periods when settlements of filed cost reports are received. Final settlements under these programs are subject to adjustment based on administrative review and audit by third party intermediaries, which can take several years to resolve completely. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The net adjustments to estimated co</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">st report settlements and other government reimbursements had the following impact to our consolidated statements of income for the years ended December 31, 2017, 2016 and 2015 (in millions, except per share amounts):</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Because the laws and regulations governing the Medicare and Medicaid programs are complex and subject to change, the estimates of contractual discounts we record could change by material amounts. A significant increase in our estimate of contractual discounts for Medicare and Medicaid would lower our earnings. This would adversely affect our results of operations, financial condition, liquidity and future access to capital.</font>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">HMOs, PPOs and Other Private Insurers</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Amounts we receive for the treatment of patients covered by HMOs, PPOs and other private insurers (collectively &#x201C;managed care plans&#x201D;) are generally less than our established billing rates. We include contractual allowances as a reduction to revenues in our consolidated fi</font><font style="display: inline;">nancial statements based on paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">specific identification and paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r specific factors for rate increases and denials. For most managed care plans, estimated contractual allowances are adjusted to actual contractual allowances as cash is received and claims are reconciled.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">If our overall estimated contractual discount percentage on our managed care program revenues for the year ended December 31, 201</font><font style="display: inline;">7 were changed by 1</font><font style="display: inline;">%, our </font><font style="display: inline;">net income</font><font style="display: inline;"> would change by approximately $</font><font style="display: inline;">56.9</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, or $</font><font style="display: inline;">1.39 per diluted share</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">This</font><font style="display: inline;"> is only one example of reasonably possible sensitivity scenarios. The process of determining the allowance requires us to estimate the amount expec</font><font style="display: inline;">ted to be received based on paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r contract provisions, historical collection data as well as other factors and requires a high degree of judgment. It is impacted by changes in managed care contracts and other related factors. A significant increase in our estimate of contractual discounts for managed care plans would lower our earnings. This would adversely affect our results of operations, financial condition, liquidity and future access to capital. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Provision and Allowance for Doubtful Accounts</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">To provide for accounts receivable that could become uncollectible in the future, we establish an allowance for doubtful accounts.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our allowance for doubtful accounts, included in our consolidated balance sheets as of </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017 and 2016</font><font style="display: inline;"> was </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">1,020.2 </font><font style="display: inline;">million and $</font><font style="display: inline;">891.2</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, respectively. Our provision for doubtful accounts, included in our consolidated results of operations for the years ended December 31, </font><font style="display: inline;">2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">, was </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">971.7</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, $</font><font style="display: inline;">909.6</font><font style="display: inline;"> million and $</font><font style="display: inline;">800.1</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, respectively.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">During the year ended December 31, 2017, we recorded an increase to our provision for doubtful accounts of $72.6 million, $46.0 million net of income taxes, or $1.13 loss per diluted share, as a result of a change in our accounting estimate of the collectability of accounts receivable.&nbsp; We are in the process of installing new systems, developing enhanced analytical procedures and updating our estimation processes in order to centralize and standardize our processes for estimating the collectability of these accounts.&nbsp; In connection with these implementation efforts, we identified additional information which indicated that our current collection estimates might be different from our historical collection estimates. We utilized this new information to further refine our estimation procedures to more precisely estimate the collectability of accounts receivable at a more detailed and disaggregated level.&nbsp; The change in our estimation procedures of the collectability of our accounts receivable is considered a change in accounting estimate in accordance with ASC 250-10.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The largest component of our allowance for doubtful accounts relates to accounts for which patients are responsible, which we refer to as patient responsibility accounts or self-pay accounts. These accounts include both amounts payable by uninsured patients and co-payments and deductibles payable by insured patients. In general, we attempt to collect deductibles, co-payments and self-pay accounts prior to the time of service for non-emergency care. If we do not collect these patient responsibility accounts prior to the delivery of care, the accounts are handled through our billing and collections processes.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

				<font style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 0pt;font-family:Symbol;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9;font-size:10pt;;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td style="width:0pt;"><p style="width:0pt;width:0pt;font-size:0pt;"></p></td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt;margin:3pt 20.9pt 0pt 0pt;">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">utilization of collection agencies; and</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="width:100%; table-layout: fixed;" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td style="width:36pt;"><p style="width:36pt;font-size:0pt;"></p></td><td valign="top" align="left" style="width: 18.00pt;">
			<p style="border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt;margin:3pt 20.9pt 0pt 0pt;">
				<font style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 0pt;font-family:Symbol;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9;font-size:10pt;;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td style="width:0pt;"><p style="width:0pt;width:0pt;font-size:0pt;"></p></td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt;margin:3pt 20.9pt 0pt 0pt;">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">if collection efforts are unsuccessful, write-off of the accounts.</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our policy is to write-off accounts after all collection efforts have failed, which is generally one year after the date of discharge of the patient. Patient responsibility accounts represent the majority of our write-offs. All of our hospitals retain third-party collection agencies for billing and collection of delinquent accounts. At most of our hospitals, more than one collection agency is used to promote competition and improve performance results. The selection of collection agencies and the timing of referral of an account to a collection agency vary among our hospitals.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We determine the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts utilizing a number of analytical tools and benchmarks. No single statistic or measurement alone determines the adequacy of the allowance. Specifically, we mo</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">nitor the revenue trends by paye</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">r classification on a month-by-month basis along with the composition of our accounts receivable agings. This review is focused primarily on trends in self-pay revenues, accounts receivable, co-payment receivables, historic payment patterns and other factors such as revenue days in accounts receivable.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;">The process of determining our allowance for doubtful accounts requires us to estimate uncollectible self-pay accounts. Our estimate of uncollectible self-pay accounts is primarily based on our collection history, adjusted for anticipated changes in collection trends, if significant. Our estimate may be impacted by changes in regional economic conditions, </font><font style="display: inline;">business office operations, paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r mix and trends in federal or state governmental </font><font style="display: inline;">healthcare co</font><font style="display: inline;">verage or other third party paye</font><font style="display: inline;">rs. </font><font style="display: inline;">If the actual self-pay collectio</font><font style="display: inline;">n percentage would change by 1.5</font><font style="display: inline;">% from our estimated self-pay collection percentage for the year ended December 31, 201</font><font style="display: inline;">7</font><font style="display: inline;">, our </font><font style="display: inline;">net income </font><font style="display: inline;">would change by approximately </font><font style="display: inline;">$7.6</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">million</font><font style="display: inline;">, or diluted earnings per share of </font><font style="display: inline;">$0.19</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">The resulting change in this analytical tool is considered to be a reasonably likely change that would</font><font style="display: inline;"> affect our overall assessment of this critical accounting estimate.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 20.9pt 12pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Goodwill Impairment Analysis</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Goodwill represents the excess of the purchase price over the fair value of the net assets of acquired businesses. Our goodwill included in our consolidated balance sheets as of </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017 and 2016</font><font style="display: inline;"> was </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">1,737.8 million </font><font style="display: inline;">and $</font><font style="display: inline;">1,777.9</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">million, resp</font><font style="display: inline;">ectively. Refer to Note 5</font><font style="display: inline;"> to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this report for a detailed rollforward of our goodwill.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In accordance with ASC 350-10, &#x201C;Intangibles&nbsp;&#x2014;&nbsp;Goodwill and Other&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC 350-10&#x201D;) goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite lives are reviewed by us at least annually for impairment. Our business comprises a single reporting unit for impairment test purposes. For the purposes of these analyses, our estimate</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> of fair value are based on a combination of the income approach, which estimates the fair value of us based on our future discounted cash flows, and the market approach, which estimates the fair value of us based on comparable market prices. Our estimate of future discounted cash flows is based on assumptions and projections we believe to be currently reasonable and supportable. Our assumptions take into account revenue and expense growth rates, </font><font style="display: inline;">patient volumes, changes in paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r mix, and chang</font><font style="display: inline;">es in legislation and other paye</font><font style="display: inline;">r payment patterns.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">If we determine the carrying value of goodwill is impaired, or if the carrying value of a business that is to be sold or otherwise disposed of exceeds its fair value, then we reduce the carrying value, including any allocated goodwill, to fair </font><font style="display: inline;">value. During the years ended </font><font style="display: inline;">December 31, 2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">, we performed our annual impairment tests as of October 1, and did not incur an impairment charge. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:9pt 20.9pt 12pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Reserves for Self-Insurance Claims</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We are subject to potential professional liability claims, employee workers&#x2019; compensation claims and other claims. To mitigate a portion of this risk, we maintain insurance for individual professional liability claims and employee workers&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;"> compensation claims exceeding </font><font style="display: inline;">self-insured retention</font><font style="display: inline;"> and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;"> level</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Our deductible level for professional liability claims is $5.0 million per claim at December 31, 2017 with a $5.0 million inner aggregate per claim.&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Additionally, </font><font style="display: inline;">we participate</font><font style="display: inline;"> in state specific professional liability programs in Indiana, Kansas, New Mexico, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. </font><font style="display: inline;">A</font><font style="display: inline;">s of December 31, 2017, our deductible level for workers&#x2019; compensation claims is $1.0 million per claim in all states in which we operate except for Wyoming. We participate in a state specific program in Wyoming for our workers&#x2019; compensation claims arising in this state. Our self-insured retention level is evaluated annually as a part of our insurance program&#x2019;s renewal process.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Each year, we obtain quotes from various insurers with respect to the cost of obtaining insurance coverage. We compare these quotes to our most recent actuarially determined estimates of losses at various self-insured retention </font><font style="display: inline;">and deductible </font><font style="display: inline;">levels. Accordingly, changes in insurance costs affect the self-insured retention</font><font style="display: inline;"> and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;"> level</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> we choose each year. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our reserves for self-insurance</font><font style="display: inline;"> and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;"> claims reflects the current estimate of all outstanding losses, including incurred but not reported losses, based upon actuarial calculations as of the balance sheet date. The loss estimates included in the actuarial calculations may change in the future based upon updated facts and circumstances. Our expense for self-insurance</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;"> claims coverage each year includes: the actuarially determined estimate of losses for the current year, including claims incurred but not reported; the change in the estimate of losses for prior years based upon actual claims development experience as compared to prior actuarial projections; the insurance premiums for losses in excess of our self-insured retention</font><font style="display: inline;"> and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;"> levels; the administrative costs of the insurance program; and interest expense related to the discounted portion of the liability.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our reserves for professional liability claims are based upon quarterly actuarial calculations. O</font><font style="display: inline;">ur reserves for employee worker</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;">&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;"> compensation claims are based upon semi</font><font style="display: inline;">-</font><font style="display: inline;">annual actuarial calculations. Our reserve calculations consider historical claims data, demographic considerations, severity factors and other actuarial assumptions, which are discounted to present value. We </font><font style="display: inline;">have discounted our reserves for self-insured claims to their present va</font><font style="display: inline;">lue using a discount rate of 1.42</font><font style="display: inline;">%, </font><font style="display: inline;">1.31</font><font style="display: inline;">% and </font><font style="display: inline;">1.35</font><font style="display: inline;">% at December 31, </font><font style="display: inline;">2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively. We select a discount rate by considering a risk-free interest rate that corresponds to the period when the self-insured claims are incurred and projected to be paid.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

				</td>

		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">As of December 31, 2017 and 2016, less than 1% of our reserves for self-insured claims represents reserves for settled and unpaid claims. Our average lag time between the settlement and payment of a self-insured claim ranges from 1 to 2 weeks.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our estimated reserves for self-insured claims will be significantly affected if current and future claims differ from historical trends. While we monitor reported claims closely and consider potential outcomes when determining our reserves for self-insured claims, the complexity of the claims, the extended period of time to settle the claims and the wide range of potential outcomes complicates the estimation process. In addition, certain states have passed varying forms of tort reform which attempt to limit the amount of awards. If such laws are passed in the states where our hospitals are located, our loss estimates could decrease.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our estimate of reserves for self-insured </font><font style="display: inline;">and deductible</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">claims are based upon actuarial calculations and are significantly influenced by key assumptions and other factors. These factors include, but are not limited to: historical paid claims; trending of loss development factors; trends in the frequency and severity of claims, which can differ significantly by jurisdiction as a result of the legislative and judicial climate in such jurisdictions; coverage limits of third-party insurance and actuarial determined statistical confidence levels. Given the number of assumptions and characteristics of each assumption considered in establishing the reserves for self-insured claims, it is difficult to compute the individual financial impact of each assumption or groups of assumptions. Some of the assumptions are dependent upon the quantitative measurement of other assumptions, and therefore are not accurately evaluated in isolation. For example, a change in the frequency of claims assumption is also affected by the estimated severity of these claims resulting in an inability to properly isolate and quantify the impact of a change in this assumption.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Professional and general liability claims are typically resolved over an extended period of time, often as long as five years or more, while workers&#x2019; compensation claims are typically resolved in one to two years. Our reserves for self-insured claims are comprised of estimated indemnity and expense payments related to reported events and incurred but not reported events as of the end of the period. We have the ability to reliably determine the amount and timing of payments based on sufficient history of our claims development, the use of external actuarial expertise and our rigorous review process. Actuarial payment patterns are based on our individual hospital historical data both prior to and after our inception in 1999. The processes, performed by both external actuaries and our management, enable us to reliably determine the amount of our ultimate losses as well as the timing of the loss settlements such that discounting of the reserves for self-insured claims is appropriate. Given the number of factors considered in establishing the reserves for self-insured claims, it is neither practical nor meaningful to isolate a particular assumption or parameter of the process and calculate the impact of changing that single item.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Ultimately, from an actuarial standpoint, the sensitivity in the estimates of reserves for self-insured claims is reflected in the various actuarial confidence levels. Our best estimate of our reserves for self-insured claims utilizes a statistical confidence level that is 50%. Higher statistical confidence levels, while not representative of our best estimate, reflect reasonably likely outcomes upon the ultimate resolution of related claims. Using a higher statistical confidence level would increase the estimated reserves for self-insured claims. </font><font style="display: inline;">A 25% increase in our utilized statistical confidence level would increase our estimated reserve by $21.7 million.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Changes in our estimates of reserves for self-insured claims are non-cash charges and accordingly, do not impact our liquidity or capital resources.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:12pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;">The combination of changing conditions and the extended time required for claim resolution results in a loss estimation process that requires actuarial skill and the application of judgment, and such estimates require periodic revision. As a result of the variety of factors that must be considered, there is a risk that actual incurred losses may develop differently from</font><font style="display: inline;"> estimates. The results of our</font><font style="display: inline;"> quarterly and semi-annual actuarial calculations resulted in changes to </font><font style="display: inline;">our</font><font style="display: inline;"> reserves for self-insured claims for prior years. </font><font style="display: inline;">As a result, for t</font><font style="display: inline;">he years ended December 31, 2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">, our related self-insured c</font><font style="display: inline;">laims expense decreased by $32.4 million, $31.0 million and $21.7</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, which increased n</font><font style="display: inline;">et income by approximately $20.6 million, $19.4 million and $13.5</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, o</font><font style="display: inline;">r $0.50, $0.45 and $0.29</font><font style="display: inline;"> per diluted share, respectively.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:11pt 0pt;text-indent:13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Accounting for Stock-Based Compensation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 11pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We issue</font><font style="display: inline;"> stock-based a</font><font style="display: inline;">wards, including stock options </font><font style="display: inline;">and other stock-based awards (nonvested stock, restricted stock, restricted stock units and performance shares) to certain officers, employees and non-employee directors in accordance with </font><font style="display: inline;">our stockholder-</font><font style="display: inline;">approved </font><font style="display: inline;">2013 Long-Term Incentive Plan, which was amended and restated effective June 6, 2017 (the &#x201C;2013 LTIP&#x201D;). </font><font style="display: inline;">We account for our stock-based awards in accordance with the provisions of ASC 718-10, &#x201C;Compensation&nbsp;&#x2014;&nbsp;Stock Compensation&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC 718-10&#x201D;) and accordingly recognize compensation expense over each of the stock-based award&#x2019;s requisite service period based on the estimated grant date fair value.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our stock-based compensation</font><font style="display: inline;"> expense </font><font style="display: inline;">was $</font><font style="display: inline;">25.4</font><font style="display: inline;"> million</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">22.0</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">million </font><font style="display: inline;">and $35.0</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">million </font><font style="display: inline;">for the years ended December 31,</font><font style="display: inline;"> 2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 11pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We estimate the fair value of stock options granted using </font><font style="display: inline;">a binomial lattice </font><font style="display: inline;">option valuation model and a single option award approach. We </font><font style="display: inline;">use a binomial lattice option valuation model </font><font style="display: inline;">because it considers characteristics of fair value option pricing, such as an option&#x2019;s contractual term and the probability of exercise before the end of the contractual term. In addition, the complications surrounding the expected term of an option are material, as indicated in ASC 718-10. Given our r</font><font style="display: inline;">elatively</font><font style="display: inline;"> large pool of un</font><font style="display: inline;">exercised options, we believe a binomial lattice option valuation model </font><font style="display: inline;">that specifically addresses this fact and models a full term of exercises is the most appropriate and reliable means of valuing our stock options. We are amortizing the fair value on a straight-line basis over the requisite service periods of the awards, which are the vesting periods of three </font><font style="display: inline;">or four </font><font style="display: inline;">years. The stock options vest </font><font style="display: inline;">at either </font><font style="display: inline;">33.3%</font><font style="display: inline;"> or 25%</font><font style="display: inline;"> on each grant anniversary date over three </font><font style="display: inline;">or four </font><font style="display: inline;">years of continued employment.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:12pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Population Stratification</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In accordance with ASC 718-10, a company should aggregate individual awards into relatively homogeneous groups with respect to exercise and post-vesting employment behaviors for the purpose of refining the expected term assumption, regardless of the valuation technique used to estimate the fair value. In addition, ASC 718-10 indicates that a company may generally make a reasonable fair value estimate with as few as one or two groupings. We have determined that a single employee population group is appropriate based on an analysis of our historical exercise patterns.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Expected Volatility</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Volatility is a measure of the tendency of investment returns to vary around a long-term average rate. Historical volatility is an appropriate starting point for setting this assumption in accordance with ASC 718-10. According to ASC 718-10, companies should also consider how future experience may differ from the past. This may require using other factors to adjust historical volatility, such as implied volatility, peer-group volatility and the range and mean-reversion of volatility estimates over various historical periods. ASC 718-10 acknowledges that there is likely to be a range of reasonable estimates for volatility. In addition, ASC 718-10 requires that if a best estimate cannot be made, management should use the mid-point in the range of reasonable estimates for volatility. We estimate the volatility of our common stock at the date of grant based on both historical volatility and implied volatility from traded options of our common stock, consistent with ASC 718-10.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Risk-Free Interest Rate</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Lattice models require risk-free interest rates for all potential times of exercise obtained by using a grant-date yield curve. A lattice model would, therefore, require the yield curve for the entire time period during which employees might exercise their options. We base the risk-free rate on the implied yield in effect at the time of option grant on </font><font style="display: inline;">U.S.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Treasury zero-coupon issues with equivalent remaining terms.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Expected Dividends</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have never paid any cash dividends on our common stock and do not anticipate paying any cash dividends in the foreseeable future. Accordingly, we use an expected dividend yield of zero.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Pre-Vesting Forfeitures</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Pre-vesting forfeitures do not affect the fair value calculation, but they affect the expense calculation. ASC 718-10 requires us to estimate pre-vesting forfeitures at the time of grant and revise those estimates in subsequent periods if actual forfeitures differ from those estimates. We use historical data to estimate pre-vesting forfeitures and record share-based compensation expense only for those awards that are expected to vest.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We apply a dynamic forfeiture rate methodology over the vesting period of the award. The dynamic forfeiture rate methodology incorporates the lapse of time into the resulting expense calculation and results in a forfeiture rate that diminishes as the granted awards approach its vest date. Accordingly, the dynamic forfeiture rate methodology results in a more consistent stock compensation expense calculation over the vesting period of the award.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Post-Vesting Cancellations</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Post-vesting cancellations include vested options that are cancelled, exercised or expire unexercised. Lattice models treat post-vesting cancellations and voluntary early exercise behavior as two separate assumptions. We use historical data to estimate post-vesting cancellations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 20.9pt 12pt 13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Expected Term</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">ASC 718-10 calls for an extinguishment calculation, dependent upon how long a granted option remains outstanding before it is fully extinguished. While extinguishment may result from exercise, it can also result from post-vesting cancellation or expiration at the contractual term. Expected term is an output in lattice models so we do not have to determine this amount.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:3pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The fair value calculations of our stock option grants are affected by assumptions that are believed to be reasonable based upon the facts and circumstances at the time of grant. Changes in our volatility estimates can materially affect the fair values of our stock option grants</font><font style="display: inline;">. If our estimated weighted-average volatility for the year ended December 31, 201</font><font style="display: inline;">7 were 10</font><font style="display: inline;">% higher, our </font><font style="display: inline;">net </font><font style="display: inline;">income would decrease by approximately $</font><font style="display: inline;">1.0</font><font style="display: inline;"> million, or $</font><font style="display: inline;">0.03</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">loss </font><font style="display: inline;">per diluted share.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:11pt 0pt 5pt;text-indent:15pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Generally, the fair value of our restricted stock unit awards is determined based on the closing price of our common stock on the trading date immediately prior to the grant date. However,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">144,535, 159,248 and 145,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> of the restricted stock units granted during the years ended December 31, </font><font style="display: inline;">2017, 2016 and 2015</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> respectively,</font><font style="display: inline;"> were performance-based </font><font style="display: inline;">restricted stock units, subject to the achievement of a combination of performance and/or market conditions. In addition to the achievement of the performance and/or market conditions, these performance-based restricted stock units are generally subject to the continuing service of the employee over the cliff-vesting period from the grant date of three or four years.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:11pt 0pt 5pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The performance condition for the targeted performance-based restricted stock units granted during the year ended December 31, 2017 is based on the Company&#x2019;s achievement of annually established targets for diluted earnings per share for each of 2017, 2018 and 2019.&nbsp;&nbsp;The performance condition for the targeted performance-based restricted stock units granted during the year ended December 31, 2016 is based on the Company&#x2019;s actual </font><font style="display: inline;">Adjusted </font><font style="display: inline;">EBITDA financial performance for hospital acquisitions completed in 2014 and 2015 compared to the pro forma </font><font style="display: inline;">Adjusted </font><font style="display: inline;">EBITDA target for this same group of hospitals.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, the </font><font style="display: inline;">market condition for the </font><font style="display: inline;">targeted performance-based restricted stock units granted during each of the year</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> ended December 31, 2017, 2016 an</font><font style="display: inline;">d 2015 are based</font><font style="display: inline;"> on the Company&#x2019;s three-year annualized total shareholder return relative to a peer group, Standard and Poor&#x2019;s Global Industry Classification Standard&#x2019;s Sub-Industry:&nbsp;&nbsp;Health Care Facilities with over $500.0 million in revenues or its equivalent.&nbsp;&nbsp;For these restricted stock units, the number of shares payable at the end of the vesting periods ranges from 0% to 200% of the targeted units based on the Company&#x2019;s actual performance</font><font style="display: inline;"> and/or market conditions</font><font style="display: inline;"> results </font><font style="display: inline;">as </font><font style="display: inline;">compared to the targets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:11pt 0pt 5pt;text-indent:15.1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
